vignette:
Mark, at 30, was always a man of the earth, his hands calloused and strong from years of shaping wood. He loved the smell of sawdust, the satisfying thud of a hammer, the precise fit of a perfectly cut joint. His work as a carpenter wasn't just a job; it was a craft, a passion he shared with his wife, Sarah, who admired his dedication and the beautiful pieces he brought to life. Their life together was steady, built on shared laughter and the quiet understanding that comes from years of companionship.

Then came the day everything shifted. It was a Tuesday, a routine commercial build. Mark was on the ground floor, cutting studs, when the air above him ripped with a sound he'll never forget - a high-pitched, metallic shriek followed by a thunderous crash. He looked up just in time to see a massive steel beam, meant for the third floor, buckle and tear away from its supports, plummeting downward. There was a cloud of dust, a collective gasp from the crew, and then the sickening sight of a mangled form beneath the debris. His colleague, a young apprentice, lay still. Mark felt a cold wave of shock wash over him, his own body frozen, useless. The image of the twisted metal and the unnatural angle of the apprentice's limbs burned itself into his mind.

In the immediate weeks that followed, the world felt like it was playing on a broken record. The screech of metal, the apprentice's name being yelled, the smell of concrete dust - these sensory fragments would ambush Mark at random, pulling him back to that moment with terrifying clarity. He'd be cutting a piece of trim in his workshop, and the whir of the saw would suddenly transform into the sound of the beam collapsing, his heart hammering against his ribs. Sleep offered no escape; nightmares of the accident, sometimes distorted and even more gruesome, left him waking in a cold sweat, the terror lingering long after the images faded. He tried to push it all away, to bury it under more work, but the thoughts persisted, a dark current beneath the surface of his awareness. He couldn't bring himself to visit the job site again, even to retrieve his tools, and he'd quickly change the channel if a news report mentioned construction accidents.

Now, months later, the acute shock has settled into a pervasive unease. Mark still feels the phantom vibrations of the crash in his chest whenever he hears a loud, sudden noise, whether it's a car backfiring or a dropped hammer. He's always on edge, scanning his surroundings, especially when he's on a job site, as if bracing himself for another catastrophe. His irritability has flared, leading to sharp words with Sarah over trivial things, which he instantly regrets, feeling a fresh wave of guilt and shame. He used to love the camaraderie of working with a crew, but now he prefers to work alone in his workshop, finding the presence of others unsettling, their movements unpredictable.

His carpentry, once a source of immense pride, now feels different. He finds himself making small, uncharacteristic errors in his measurements, his focus fractured. He'll stare at a half-finished project, the intricate details blurring, his mind replaying the accident for the hundredth time. The joy he once found in transforming raw wood into something beautiful has waned, replaced by a sense of obligation. He feels disconnected, a barrier between himself and the world, and most acutely, between himself and Sarah. She tries to reach him, to talk about what he's going through, but he often just shrugs or changes the subject, feeling a profound emotional numbness that prevents him from truly engaging. He sees the worry etched on her face and feels a crushing weight of being a burden, a shadow of the man he once was. He still wakes up most nights, his mind racing, his body tense, the memory of that Tuesday forever etched into the fabric of his days.
